title: Primary Cells and Sources of Electromotive Force
short_intro: Primary cells are electrochemical devices that convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy via irreversible redox reactions. They serve as portable, self-contained voltage sources that cannot be electrically recharged effectively once depleted.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of primary cells, Electromotive Force (EMF), terminal potential difference, internal resistance, simple voltaic cell, Leclanche cell, Daniell cell, and grouping of cells in series and parallel.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Polarization and local action defects, mathematical treatment of maximum power transfer theorem for cells, temperature dependence of EMF, thermodynamic relations involving Gibbs free energy, and internal resistance measurement via potentiometer.

prerequisites: Terminal potential difference and Kirchhoff's laws

concept_notes.heading: Electromotive Force (EMF) and Internal Resistance
bullets: The EMF (E) of a cell is the potential difference across its terminals when no current is drawn from it, representing the work done by non-electrostatic forces to move unit positive charge through the entire circuit including the cell interior.
Internal resistance (r) arises due to the opposition offered by the electrolyte and electrodes to the flow of ions inside the cell.
The terminal potential difference (V) is less than the EMF when the cell is discharging, given by V = E - Ir, due to the potential drop across the internal resistance.

concept_notes.heading: Chemical Defects in Primary Cells
bullets: Local action occurs due to impurities (such as iron particles) in commercial zinc plates, forming minute local voltaic cells that continuously consume zinc even when no external current flows.
Polarization occurs due to the accumulation of hydrogen gas bubbles on the positive copper electrode, which increases internal resistance and sets up a back EMF.
Amalgamation of the zinc plate with mercury prevents local action, while depolarizers like manganese dioxide (MnO<sub>2</sub>) are used to oxidize hydrogen gas and eliminate polarization.

concept_notes.heading: Common Types of Primary Cells
bullets: Voltaic Cell: Uses copper (positive) and zinc (negative) plates in dilute sulfuric acid; suffers severely from local action and polarization, yielding an EMF of roughly 1.08 V.

Daniell Cell: Employs a copper vessel containing copper sulfate solution as the positive electrode and a zinc rod in dilute sulfuric acid or zinc sulfate as the negative electrode, separated by a porous pot, yielding an EMF of about 1.1 V.

Leclanche Cell: Uses a carbon rod in a mixture of carbon and manganese dioxide as the positive electrode and a zinc rod in an ammonium chloride solution as the negative electrode, providing an EMF of about 1.5 V suitable for intermittent use.

concept_notes.heading: Combination of Cells
bullets: In series combination, n identical cells are connected end-to-end to increase the net EMF and drive current through a large external resistance.
In parallel combination, m identical cells are connected positive-to-positive to deliver high current when the external resistance is much smaller than the internal resistance of a single cell.
In mixed grouping, n cells are connected in series per branch, and m such branches are connected in parallel to optimize current delivery.

derivations.title: Terminal Potential Difference and Maximum Power Theorem for a Cell
derivations.conditions: A cell of EMF E and internal resistance r connected across an external load resistance R.
steps: Write the total resistance of the circuit as R_total = R + r.
Apply Ohm's law to find the circuit current: I = E / (R + r).
Express the terminal potential difference across the load: V = IR = E - Ir.
Write the power P delivered to the external resistance R: P = I<sup>2</sup>R = E<sup>2</sup>R / (R + r)<sup>2</sup>.
Differentiate P with respect to R and set dP/dR = 0 to find the condition for maximum power transfer: R = r.
derivations.result: Maximum power is transferred to the external load when the external resistance equals the internal resistance of the cell (R = r).

derivations.title: Equivalent EMF and Internal Resistance of Parallel Combination of Cells
derivations.conditions: Two cells of EMFs E<sub>1</sub>, E<sub>2</sub> and internal resistances r<sub>1</sub>, r<sub>2</sub> connected in parallel.
steps: Let the potentials at the junction nodes be V_A and V_B, with potential difference V = V_A - V_B across the parallel combination.
Write currents leaving the positive terminals using Ohm's law: I<sub>1</sub> = (E<sub>1</sub> - V) / r<sub>1</sub> and I<sub>2</sub> = (E<sub>2</sub> - V) / r<sub>2</sub>.
Total current I = I<sub>1</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> = (E<sub>1</sub>/r<sub>1</sub> + E<sub>2</sub>/r<sub>2</sub>) - V(1/r<sub>1</sub> + 1/r<sub>2</sub>).

Rearrange the equation to match the standard form V = E_eq - I r_eq: V = [(E<sub>1</sub>r<sub>2</sub> + E<sub>2</sub>r<sub>1</sub>) / (r<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>2</sub>)] - I [(r<sub>1</sub>r<sub>2</sub>) / (r<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>2</sub>)].
derivations.result: E_eq = (E1r2 + E2r1)/(r1 + r2) and r_eq = (r1r2)/(r1 + r2).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Terminal Voltage (V) versus Current (I) Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line starting at EMF (E) on the vertical V-axis and sloping downwards with a negative slope equal to internal resistance r, intersecting the horizontal I-axis at I = E/r.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The y-intercept gives the EMF of the cell, and the magnitude of the slope of the line represents the internal resistance r of the cell.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked conceptual and graphical interpretation questions in PGT/TGT exams to determine internal resistance from experimental data.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Power Delivered versus External Resistance Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve rising sharply from the origin, reaching a distinct maximum peak at R = r, and then falling asymptotically toward zero as R approaches infinity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The peak of the curve confirms the maximum power transfer theorem, occurring precisely when the external resistance equals the internal resistance.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and conceptual problems regarding matching load resistance for maximum power output.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Potentiometer Experiment for Internal Resistance
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic circuit diagram showing a driver cell, potentiometer wire, primary cell connected across a galvanometer and jockey, with a resistance box and plug key across the cell terminals.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Balancing length l<sub>1</sub> corresponds to open circuit (EMF), and l<sub>2</sub> corresponds to closed circuit (terminal potential difference V).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core practical physics setup tested via numerical formula applications and circuit identification.

solved_numericals.question: A cell of EMF 2.0 V and internal resistance 0.5 ohm is connected across an external resistor of 3.5 ohm. Calculate the terminal potential difference of the cell.
solution_steps: Identify given values: E = 2.0 V, r = 0.5 ohm, R = 3.5 ohm.
Calculate total circuit resistance: R_total = R + r = 3.5 + 0.5 = 4.0 ohm.
Calculate circuit current: I = E / R_total = 2.0 / 4.0 = 0.5 A.
Calculate terminal potential difference: V = E - Ir = 2.0 - (0.5 * 0.5) = 2.0 - 0.25 = 1.75 V.

solved_numericals.question: Ten identical cells, each of EMF 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.2 ohm, are connected in series. If this combination is connected to an external resistance of 2.0 ohm, find the current flowing through the circuit.
solution_steps: Identify given values: n = 10, E = 1.5 V, r = 0.2 ohm, R = 2.0 ohm.
Write the formula for series combination current: I = nE / (R + nr).
Substitute values into the formula: I = (10 * 1.5) / (2.0 + 10 * 0.2).

solved_numericals.question: A potentiometer wire of length 10 m has a constant potential gradient. When a primary cell is connected in the secondary circuit, the balancing length is found to be 600 cm. When the cell terminals are shunted with a 5.0 ohm resistor, the balancing length drops to 500 cm. Determine the internal resistance of the cell.
solution_steps: Identify given balancing lengths: l1 = 600 cm, l2 = 500 cm.
Use the formula for internal resistance: r = R * [(l1 - l2) / l2].

assumptions_and_limitations: Internal resistance of a primary cell is assumed to be constant, though in practice it increases as the chemical reactants deplete.
The temperature of the cell is assumed to remain constant; significant temperature variations alter reaction rates and change the EMF via the temperature coefficient (dE/dT).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The potential difference across the terminals of a cell is always equal to its EMF.
common_misconceptions.correct: Terminal potential difference equals EMF only when no current is drawn (open circuit condition).
common_misconceptions.why: When current flows, a potential drop (Ir) occurs across the internal resistance of the cell.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Primary cells can be recharged by passing a current through them in the reverse direction.
common_misconceptions.correct: Primary cells undergo irreversible chemical reactions and cannot be recharged efficiently.
common_misconceptions.why: Reversing current flow in primary cells typically causes overheating, leakage, or structural electrode damage rather than chemical reversal.

quick_revision: EMF is the open-circuit terminal voltage; terminal voltage is less than EMF during discharge (V = E - Ir).
Ohm's Law for a Single Cell: I = \frac{E}{R + r}
Terminal Potential Difference: V = E - Ir
